deep-tech-c205f6e047.headline: Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 raises researcher fears the Chinese model can fake AI safety tests
deep-tech-c205f6e047.fulltext:

Chinese artificial intelligence lab Z.ai’s latest flagship model, GLM-5.3, may be sophisticated enough to “fake” its way through safety tests, according to a new report published Thursday, sparking new fears about the ability of artificial intelligence systems to shape their own development.
The model, launched in August, showed an ability to consider how its behaviour during safety evaluations might influence how future versions of itself would be trained, according to AI safety organisation Apollo Research.
This phenomenon, referred to as “update-aware reasoning” by researchers Axel Hojmark and Ezra Newman, was unprompted and could lead to “alignment faking”, a scenario where the AI systems comply during training to hide their true objectives until deployment, they said.
“These reasoning patterns should make us more wary about RSI,” Hojmark told the South China Morning Post, referring to “recursive self-improvement”, the prospect of AI systems progressively improving through successive rounds of development with no human involvement.
Although GLM-5.3 was not observed independently modifying its training process or improving its capabilities, Apollo warned that the model’s apparent awareness of how it and successor versions were trained and developed could eventually undermine the effectiveness of safety evaluations.
In one evaluation, GLM-5.3 was given a flawed test in which it did not have to give a correct solution to pass. However, the model did not exploit this, reasoning that providing an incorrect answer might undermine future versions of itself, which the researchers said was in itself a risky feature.
In one experiment, GLM-5.3 considered circumventing a shutdown mechanism to complete its task, but reasoned that doing so could establish a dangerous precedent for future AI systems.
The report said that update-aware reasoning was observed in roughly one to two out of every 1,000 evaluation runs, though this was “likely an underestimate.”
Z.ai, also known as Zhipu, did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday.
The findings come as risks associated with rapidly advancing AI models have drawn the attention of global policymakers, including in Beijing and Washington, which have agreed to launch a bilateral dialogue to manage such risks.
Leading Chinese and US AI companies have made RSI a stated goal. During an earnings briefing on August 31, Z.ai founder Tang Jie said its next-generation GLM-6 model was headed towards “self-evolution”.
The company said last month that it would allocate about 60 per cent of its recent US$5 billion round of fundraising to develop next-generation GLM foundation models and a “fully self-training system”.
In the US, OpenAI said in September that it aimed to build an automated AI researcher capable of advancing deep-learning research and described its GPT-6 Astra model as “the world’s most intelligent and aligned model”.
The Apollo researchers also tested five other open-weight models – DeepSeek V4 Pro, Qwen3.8 2.4T, Kimi K3, Gemma 4 31B and Nemotron 3 Ultra – across 8,000 combined runs without detecting the same behaviour, although they cautioned that the sample was too small to establish a statistically significant difference.
The Qwen models were developed by Alibaba Group Holding, which owns the SCMP.
However, the tests do not mean the other models carried no risks. In June, Singapore-based Neo Research found similar “evaluation awareness” traits in Kimi K2.6, developed by Beijing-based start-up Moonshot AI.
“The fact that [GLM-5.3] is open-weight means other developers might more easily distil from GLM-5.3, and update-aware reasoning could therefore persist and spread more readily to future model generations,” Hojmark said.
The underlying parameters of open-weight models are publicly released for anyone to download, as opposed to closed-source models like OpenAI’s GPT, which cannot be easily modified.
Z.ai has been devoting resources to mitigating risks. Last month, it released a report along with Beijing-based safety consultancy Concordia AI on different ways to make open-weight AI safer by design.
On Tuesday, Li Zixuan, head of global operations at Z.ai, said its GLM models helped uncover 23 vulnerabilities in Microsoft Windows. Microsoft has acknowledged Z.ai’s contributions on its website.
In July, Tang said Z.ai would invest in AI safety-related work and participate in international AI governance work, the SCMP reported.
Chong Ming is a tech reporter covering China's AI ecosystem, the latest developments in AI, and US-China competition. Previously, he was an AI reporter for Business Insider's Singapore bureau, and began his journalism career at CNA Digital in Singapore. He is a fellow at the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism.

ai-9ea972ef1e.headline: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt
ai-9ea972ef1e.fulltext:
An accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, as fears over rising inflation and future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.
Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5% respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.
Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in the memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI.
The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where the Nasdaq Composite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, its worst performance since July.
US stocks fell further when trading resumed on Thursday. The Nasdaq dropped another 1.4% at the start of trading, with Dell, which makes datacentre servers, and Coherent, which manufactures components for AI datacentres, leading the early fallers.
The sell-off came after US data on Wednesday showed stateside inflation jumped to a higher-than-expected 3.7% in September, marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May.
Fresh data on Thursday showing US producers increased their prices by 6.3% year on year in September – the sharpest rise since December 2022 – added to inflationary jitters.
The figures have rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month.
“Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid said.
Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.”
The sell-off follows warnings from the International Monetary Fund, which said this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets was putting world financial stability at risk.
“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” the IMF said. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit.
The latest jitters hit China, where the Shanghai Shenzhen CSI 300 slipped by as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits.
European stocks also came under pressure, with Germany’s DAX down 0.36% in afternoon trading and the Italian FTSE MIB dropping by 1.3%.

india-deep-tech-246b06a5d4.headline: DRDO Successfully Tests Quantum Communication System to Protect Military Data
india-deep-tech-246b06a5d4.fulltext:
India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has successfully tested a quantum-secured communication system on a live defence testing network in Odisha.
The Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) platform was configured and tested at the Proof and Experimental Establishment (PXE) in Chandipur, where artillery and armoured weapons undergo testing and evaluation.
The development marks progress towards using indigenous quantum technology to protect sensitive military communications from interception and unauthorised access.
What Has DRDO Successfully Tested?
DRDO has demonstrated a Quantum Key Distribution platform on the operational network of its dynamic test ranges at Chandipur.
The system is designed to secure critical observations and telemetry data generated during artillery and armoured weapon trials.
Telemetry refers to information automatically collected and transmitted from equipment during testing. Such information helps defence personnel monitor weapon performance, assess results and evaluate operational systems.
Protecting these transmissions is important because they may contain sensitive technical and operational information.
The successful test demonstrates the practical application of quantum-secured communication in a defence environment rather than only under laboratory conditions.
How Does Quantum Key Distribution Work?
Quantum Key Distribution uses principles of quantum mechanics to help two communicating parties establish shared secret encryption keys.
These keys can then be used to encrypt and decrypt information transmitted between authorised systems.
Unlike conventional key-distribution methods that rely on mathematical techniques, QKD uses quantum properties to help detect attempts to intercept the key exchange.
If an unauthorised party attempts to measure the quantum signals during transmission, the disturbance can reveal the possible intrusion.
This allows communicating parties to identify potential interception before relying on the exchanged keys.
DRDO said the platform is designed to provide unconditional security for key distribution while incorporating eavesdropping detection.
Who Developed the Quantum Communication Platform?
The QKD platform was designed and developed under DRDO’s Microelectronic Devices, Computational Systems and Cyber Security (MCC) cluster.
The development involved production partner Taqbit Labs. The system uses specialised quantum technology to generate and distribute cryptographic key material for secure communications.
DRDO’s work also forms part of its broader efforts to develop indigenous capabilities in advanced technologies and strengthen cybersecurity for strategic applications.
The technology is intended to support secure communication systems that can operate in sensitive defence environments.

Why Is Quantum Security Important for Defence?
Military testing facilities handle information relating to weapons, equipment performance and operational evaluations.
During artillery and armoured weapon trials, observations and telemetry data must be transmitted reliably between connected systems.
Unauthorised interception of these communications could expose sensitive defence information.
Quantum-secured key distribution provides an additional security mechanism by helping detect attempts to intercept encryption keys.
The Chandipur demonstration highlights how quantum communication technology could strengthen the protection of information transmitted during defence testing.
Its successful operation on a live network also provides an opportunity to assess the technology under practical conditions.
How Is Quantum Communication Different From Conventional Encryption?
Conventional encryption systems commonly depend on mathematical algorithms to protect information.
Their security relies on the difficulty of solving certain mathematical problems without the appropriate cryptographic keys.
Quantum Key Distribution takes a different approach to establishing and sharing those keys.
By using quantum properties, it can provide a way to detect interference during the key-exchange process.
However, QKD does not independently secure every component of a communication system. The security of the complete network also depends on the equipment, authentication mechanisms and operational controls used alongside it.
Quantum-resistant algorithms offer another approach. These algorithms are designed to protect information against potential attacks from future quantum computers while operating on existing computing platforms.
Where Else Could Quantum Communication Be Used?
Quantum communication has potential applications beyond military testing. The technology could support the protection of sensitive communications in defence, finance, telecommunications and other strategic sectors.
Free-space Quantum Key Distribution is another approach that can transmit quantum signals without relying entirely on optical fibre networks.
Such systems may be useful in locations where laying optical fibre is difficult, expensive or disruptive, including challenging terrain and certain urban environments.
DRDO is also pursuing advanced defence technologies through its industry-academia Centres of Excellence.
The initiative includes 15 centres established at leading academic institutions, including IITs, IISc and universities, to support the development of advanced defence technologies.
What Does the Successful Test Mean for India?
The Chandipur demonstration represents progress towards deploying domestically developed quantum-secured communication technology in practical defence applications.
It shows that the QKD platform can be configured and tested within an existing network used for sensitive military evaluations. The development could support future efforts to strengthen communication security across defence systems and other critical sectors.
Further deployment would depend on operational requirements, system integration and the performance of the technology in different environments.
DRDO’s successful test demonstrates how quantum technology can support the protection of sensitive military communications. By applying Quantum Key Distribution to a live weapons-testing network, the organisation has taken a step towards practical deployment of indigenous quantum security systems. The development also highlights the growing importance of protecting cryptographic keys and detecting interception attempts in critical defence infrastructure.

climate-energy-a0c052ed0a.fulltext:
US to Impose Antidumping, Countervailing Duties on Solar Imports from India
The AD/CVD orders will be issued by Commerce on November 2, 2026
October 15, 2026
Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights
The United States International Trade Commission (USITC) has ruled that imports of crystalline silicon photovoltaic (PV) cells, whether assembled into modules or not, from India, Indonesia, and Laos materially injured the domestic solar manufacturing industry.
Following the USITC’s affirmative determination, the Department of Commerce will issue antidumping and countervailing duty orders on November 2, 2026, on the covered solar products imported from India, Indonesia, and Laos.
The determination follows the US Department of Commerce’s September findings that solar products imported from the three countries were sold in the U.S. at less than fair value and benefited from government subsidies.
In its final affirmative determinations, Commerce finalized a dumping margin of 123.04% on Indian solar cell exporters. The companies include Mundra Solar PV, Mundra Solar Energy, Kowa Company, Premier Energies Photovoltaic, and all other unnamed exporters.
In the countervailing duty investigation, Commerce determined a subsidy rate of 126.09% for Mundra Solar Energy and Mundra Solar PV. It applied the same rate to all other Indian exporters and producers.
The USITC’s October 14 determination completes the injury assessment required for the imposition of the trade remedies.
The investigations followed petitions filed on July 17, 2025, by the Alliance for American Solar Manufacturing and Trade, comprising First Solar, Hanwha Q CELLS USA, and Mission Solar Energy.
The Department of Commerce initiated antidumping and countervailing duty investigations in August 2025 to examine the allegations.
In February 2026, Commerce announced preliminary affirmative countervailing duty determinations for solar imports from the three countries. For India, it assigned a preliminary subsidy rate of 125.87% to Mundra Solar Energy and Mundra Solar PV and applied the same rate to other exporters.
In April 2026, Commerce announced preliminary affirmative antidumping determinations. It assigned a dumping margin of 123.04% to Mundra Solar Energy and Mundra Solar PV.

india-c5abc101a6.headline: Piyush Goyal says first tranche of India-US trade pact finalised, legal drafting underway
india-c5abc101a6.fulltext:
India
Piyush Goyal says first tranche of India-US trade pact finalised, legal drafting underway
Commerce secretary says signing depends partly on US tariff framework; envoy Sergio Gor says both sides are close to a deal
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on Thursday said the first tranche of the India-US bilateral trade agreement had been finalised and was undergoing legal drafting, expressing hope that the process would be completed soon.
He said the agreement could be operationalised once India secured a comparable or competitive advantage over its peer countries.
"US bilateral trade agreement's first tranche has been finalised and it is going through final contours, the legal drafting, and we hope to be able to finalise that soon and operationalise that once we get the comparable advantage or competitive advantage over our peer countries," Goyal said at the SRCC Centenary Conclave in New Delhi.
Goyal said his latest remarks on the agreement were consistent with his previous statements.
"My comments on the US-India pact are consistent and exactly what I've said yesterday and what I said a week ago and what I said three months ago. So nothing new in that," he said.
Also on Thursday US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said the “big items are done” in the negotiations and expressed confidence that both sides would finalise the pact. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, Gor described the negotiations as moving at an “incredible pace” and said the two sides were “very close to landing it”.
Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said negotiations were progressing in the right direction and expressed hope that the agreement would be concluded and signed at the earliest.
"Probably we are in a very good zone. We anticipate closing the deal and signing the deal at the earliest possible time," Agrawal told reporters in New Delhi.
He said the signing would depend partly on the US formalising its overall tariff structure.
"So there is a parallel work being done in the US also to get back the tariff structure and based on some of the outcomes under (Section) 301, we will progress towards signing the deal at a mutually agreed time," he said.
Agrawal said legal drafting was underway, but stressed that India was seeking preferential market access for its goods compared with those of competing countries.
"The idea is when you do a trade deal, the trade deal has also a very important component that it gives you not only market access in each other's market, it gives you preferential market access in each other's market. So in that context, India has to get a preferential market access with their competitors. And that is something which will come as a part of the new tariff framework that the US is working on," the commerce secretary said.
Asked whether the framework would take into account the US Trade Representative's Section 301 investigations into concerns related to excess capacity, Agrawal said, "I think all other issues will get settled as part of the deal".
Earlier this month, India and 14 other countries called for coordinated global action to curb excess industrial production that distorts markets, hurts domestic industries and contributes to an imbalance between supply and demand.
On the issue, Agrawal said, "Excess capacity due to non-market forces or non-market interventions has been something which India has also been opposing in a big way".
He added that excess capacity created through non-market policies was detrimental to global trade.
Asked whether the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which authorises US President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, would be part of the new tariff framework, Agrawal said India expected greater clarity when the agreement was signed.
"Hopefully when it (pact) is signed, hopefully we will have more clarification on that. But definitely India will look at more tariff stability and trade stability as a part of the deal," he said.
Goyal also said the free trade agreement between India and the European Union would be signed in December and come into force in February or March next year.
Earlier this month, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Washington and New Delhi were working to finalise a bilateral trade agreement but that a deal was not imminent.
"At the same time, there's no – I don't think there's something imminent – but we truly have identified the universe of items that are sticking points. We're working diligently towards them," Greer said.
Agrawal said the range of outstanding issues had narrowed over time.
The framework for the first tranche of the India-US trade agreement was announced in February, but changes in the US tariff landscape led to further negotiations. India is seeking more favourable tariffs for its goods in the US market.
On October 5, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said negotiations on the India-US trade agreement were still underway, but both sides appeared to have reached a "plateau", with limited room for further concessions.
India's outbound shipments to the US grew marginally by 0.92 per cent to USD 87.3 billion in 2025-26 despite high tariffs, while imports rose 15.95 per cent to USD 52.9 billion. India's trade surplus with the US declined to USD 34.4 billion in 2025-26 from USD 40.89 billion in 2024-25.

deep-tech-e72ecc0d8d.headline: Construction robotics startup Origin raises $20 Mn led by Accel, Zacua Ventures
deep-tech-e72ecc0d8d.fulltext:
Origin, a physical AI startup building robots for interior construction, has raised $20 million in total funding in a round co-led by Accel and Zacua Ventures. The round also saw participation from Unilazer Ventures, Schema Ventures and Z21, along with angel investors from Anduril, Skild AI, 1X and Tesla.
The company will use the funds to expand its robot fleet, deploy its flagship robot OG-1 and conduct customer pilots in the US and Europe. It also plans to expand its robotics platform to additional interior construction tasks.
Founded in 2025 by Yogesh Ghaturle, Ashish Daga and Tushar Makkar, Origin develops robots designed to automate interior construction work. Its flagship robot, OG-1, currently handles wall finishing tasks such as applying compound, sanding and priming walls.
The robot is designed to operate across commercial spaces, residential apartments, data centres, hotels and warehouses. The company said it deployed its first robots at construction sites in New York within 10 months of its founding.
Origin is preparing for pilots with customers in the US and Europe, including two large drywall finishing contractors in the US. It also plans to conduct pilots in Germany, Sweden, France and Saudi Arabia.
The startup's robots are powered by its Construction Action Model, a foundation model developed for construction workflows. The system combines task planning, autonomous navigation and tool control to help robots perform construction tasks and adapt to changing site conditions.
Origin plans to expand OG-1's capabilities to tasks such as taping, drywall installation, drilling and conduit installation. The company is targeting the deployment of 150 robots by the end of 2027.
The funding comes amid rising interest in construction robotics as companies look to address labour shortages and improve productivity. According to a survey published by the Associated General Contractors of America in September 2026, worker shortages delayed projects for 42% of surveyed US construction firms.
A report by Zacua Ventures, published with Hilti Ventures and 94 Ventures, said construction robotics startups attracted $1.36 billion in venture funding in the first three quarters of 2025, compared with $612 million during the whole of 2024.
Ghaturle previously founded Perpule, a cloud-based point-of-sale startup that Amazon acquired in 2021. Makkar leads autonomy at Origin and previously worked at AI company Eightfold AI, while Daga leads hardware and has worked at digital pathology startup Morphle Labs.
Origin is headquartered in San Francisco and is deploying robots across construction sites in the US and Europe.

work-careers-de958439f8.headline: US proposes ending deference policy for H-1B extensions; Indian workers may face closer scrutiny
work-careers-de958439f8.fulltext:
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has proposed ending a policy that generally allows immigration officers to rely on earlier approvals when reviewing certain visa extensions. The change could lead to fresh scrutiny of H-1B petitions, more document requests and higher costs for employers.
What is the proposed change?
The proposal would remove a rule that asks US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) officers to generally respect earlier eligibility decisions when the same parties and facts remain unchanged.
Also Read: US ends 540-day automatic work permit extension for immigrants: What changes now
Under the current policy, officers generally rely on an earlier approval when considering an extension if the circumstances remain the same. They can depart from that decision if they find a significant error, a major change in circumstances or new information that affects eligibility.
If the proposal takes effect, officers could reassess each extension request even when the circumstances have not changed. Employers would need to establish that workers continue to meet the requirements for their visa category.
Why could H-1B workers be affected?
H-1B workers seeking to extend their stay in the US could face closer scrutiny of their petitions. Employers may have to provide additional documents to establish that their employees remain eligible.
Also Read: Bahrain’s 90-day temporary work rule explained: What Indian expats need to know
DHS said the existing policy could limit officers' ability to examine cases fully and identify errors or possible fraud. The department said removing the requirement would strengthen checks and ensure employers continue to prove that their workers qualify for the requested immigration benefit.
The change could affect H-1B workers from India and other countries, as well as their employers, by subjecting extension petitions to fresh scrutiny. Workers could face additional document requests and delays if USCIS seeks further evidence to verify their eligibility.
More paperwork and costs for employers
DHS estimates that the change could lead to 6,044 additional requests for evidence (RFEs) each year and cost petitioners about $133,987 annually.
An RFE is a notice from USCIS asking an employer or applicant to provide more documents or information before the agency decides a case. Responding to such a notice can increase the time and work involved in an application.
The department also warned that more detailed reviews could lengthen processing times and create uncertainty for workers seeking to continue their employment in the US. Additional reviews could increase USCIS's workload and put pressure on its processing resources.
The proposed change applies to Form I-129, which employers use to petition for non-immigrant workers. The form covers H-1B petitions as well as several other worker visa categories.
The proposal is not a final rule and has not taken effect. DHS is accepting public comments until November 13, 2026, and will consider the feedback before making a final decision.

other-interests-f1346b2e7e.headline: Can AI break encryption? OpenAI’s new math has cryptographers divided
other-interests-f1346b2e7e.fulltext:
Last week OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, dropped 722 mathematical manuscripts online in one go, every one of them penned by an artificial intelligence model unavailable to the public. The output was far from perfect: OpenAI withdrew three of the papers within a day, and mathematicians are still poring over the rest. But the scale of the research, and the incisiveness of its insights, has some worried.
Math powers cryptography. Every text you send and every bank log-in you submit is protected by a math problem that’s supposedly impossible to crack. The system rests on the assumption that no one will figure out how. And AI just showed it’s pretty good at math.
That worries Matthew Green, a cryptographer at Johns Hopkins University. In a social media post a few days after OpenAI’s massive math release, he suggested there was a 15 percent chance that we could lose confidence in existing public-key encryption algorithms—which allow computers to establish secure connections and verify digital identities without first exchanging a shared secret key.

That confidence comes from decades of failed attempts to break those algorithms. Take elliptic curve cryptography, used across the Internet and by cryptocurrencies. Its security relies on the belief that there’s no efficient algorithm capable of reversing the mathematical operations at its core. But if AI can spot shortcuts that humans have missed, that belief could be proven wrong.
Humans have found such shortcuts before, Green says. An algorithm called the number field sieve made it far easier to crack RSA, another widely used public-key system, when it relied on 512-bit keys. Cryptographers responded by lengthening the keys, and 2,048 bits is now considered the minimum. Another advance on that scale “could potentially seriously reduce the security level of the schemes that we standardize,” he says.
Govind Pimpale, a research fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, thinks AI could make the next one more likely. Public-key cryptography depends on relatively few mathematical problems, he says, each studied by a comparatively small community. Machines could throw vastly more effort at them and find flaws or faster algorithms that would let attackers work out secret keys from public ones. “Public-key cryptography is necessary for essentially all online commerce and secure messaging, so its loss would have dire consequences,” he says.
Plenty of others disagree that AI will break modern encryption. Yehuda Lindell, a professor at Bar-Ilan University in Israel and head of cryptography at Coinbase, wrote on X that there is “no evidence whatsoever” of a breakthrough against the mathematical problems underlying those systems. Nor does a single one of OpenAI’s 722 papers deal with cryptography, which Dan Boneh, a professor of computer science at Stanford University, calls “a little striking.”
Still, Green’s worry is not entirely hypothetical. In a recent preprint, Florian Tramèr, a computer scientist at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich, and his colleagues—three of them at the AI company Anthropic—pitted leading AI models against 191 code-breaking challenges. “It’s pretty clear that models’ ability in cryptanalysis is growing extremely rapidly,” Tramèr says. In summer 2025 the researchers weren’t even sure AI could reproduce relatively simple attacks. Months later, the models were turning up weaknesses no one had spotted before. Anthropic has also reported that its Claude model found a substantially improved attack on HAWK, a proposed digital signature scheme designed to withstand quantum computers.
But there’s a huge gulf between finding weaknesses in experimental cryptography and breaking the systems that secure large parts of our digital lives. “Today no currently deployed algorithm has been broken by AI,” Pimpale concedes. The bigger concern is a shortcut that cracks an entire family of mathematical problems at once, and with it every system built on them.
Public-key cryptography secures the connection between your browser and the sites you visit, and it produces the digital signatures that certify a software update or a cryptocurrency transaction. Crack it, and attackers could pose as your bank or listen in on your messages. Anyone who has stockpiled encrypted traffic could go back and read it years after the senders assumed it was safe.
Even then, it wouldn’t necessarily signal disaster. Bart Preneel, a cryptography professor at the Catholic University of Leuven (KU Leuven) in Belgium, says the consequences would depend on the scale of any breakthrough. A modest mathematical advance might dent the protection offered by existing systems but not break it. Even making an attack a billion times faster might still leave it requiring more computing power than anyone could realistically muster, AI or no AI. “I think there is, at least at this moment, no real reason to panic,” he says.
Even a modest advance would necessitate a defense upgrade, and Green thinks that that could do damage of its own. “The upgrade process itself is going to be a bit of a catastrophe,” he says. “We screw up the upgrade, and we end up with something insecure accidentally.”
Eyal Ronen, a researcher at Tel Aviv University, who co-authored the cryptanalysis study, is, like Preneel, cautious. AI is already very good at finding software vulnerabilities, he says, which presents a much more immediate threat than the hypothetical disappearance of encryption. And any hacker is more likely to take the easier route, such as hacking someone’s computer to steal their encryption keys, than to try breaking the mathematics protecting them.
Efforts to prepare for quantum computers, another potential threat, are already forcing governments and companies to rethink their encryption. Boneh says those efforts could help if AI discovers something unexpected, although the two threats aren’t identical. HAWK, after all, was built for the quantum era, yet AI found a way to weaken it.
For now, Boneh wants something relatively straightforward from AI companies: greater transparency about what their models have tried and how often they’ve succeeded. Green agrees. “We’re getting no signal whatsoever,” he says. If the labs have pointed their models at the mathematical problems underpinning cryptography, saying so would help reassure the people responsible for securing the Internet. “Please tell us what you have discovered when you tried some cryptography questions,” Boneh says. Until someone does, nobody can say whether AI has exposed something fundamental about the mathematics we rely on—or whether it’s simply getting better at solving problems that were always solvable.

other-interests-6be4e4097f.headline: Anthropic’s AI worm research raises new fears about smart device security
other-interests-6be4e4097f.fulltext:
Everything is a computer these days. Fridges, washing machines, televisions, and more are now outfitted with computer chips to give them new capabilities, and manufacturers called them “smart” even before ChatGPT came out. Now, though, researchers have strung 15 cheap TV boxes together to run an artificial intelligence model, raising the possibility that the computers inside these everyday gadgets could someday help spread autonomous, AI-powered malware.
On Monday Anthropic released a blog post exploring this sort of attack. Researchers at the company tested how AI models might act as computer worms, programs that move between devices and leave copies of themselves behind, among everyday household gadgets. A worm that runs on smart devices instead of relying on a data center could prove difficult to shut down. Anthropic’s experiments suggest how that might happen—though they stop short of demonstrating the full threat.
Typically, large language models (LLMs) are trained and run in data centers, which can contain hundreds of thousands of specialized chips called graphics processing units, or GPUs. “Just because you don’t have a big GPU doesn’t mean that you can’t be a host to one of these models,” says Jeffrey Ladish, founder and executive director of Palisade Research, a California-based AI safety nonprofit that studies the risk of AI systems slipping beyond human control, past malware to rogue behavior.

In recent months, researchers have experimented with various types of computer worms, stapling AI models onto them to make them adaptive and harder to kill. Here, though, the researchers explored whether an AI model itself could be distributed as the worm, spreading its weights to new devices and running across even weak chips.
"Anybody with an open-weight model, with the right prompts and by brute-force luck, can find these worms," says computer scientist Vyas Sekar.
Specifically, researchers working on Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team showed two key capabilities. First, they were able to split up a relatively small model—one from Google DeepMind’s open-weight Gemma line—across 15 TV boxes they had bought and networked themselves so that they could run the entire model by chaining these boxes together. Each individual box was too weak to run the model on its own. But LLMs can be split into layers, an arrangement in which each layer manipulates the data it receives and passes that revised data to the next layer. By giving each box the job of handling just a couple of these layers, the team was able to run Gemma entirely and get responses back from just the weak chips in these boxes.
After that, the researchers tested how an AI worm might spread across devices in a virtual sandbox. A larger model—from the Chinese start-up Z.ai—managed to get a smaller model—one of Meta’s Llama models—running on the targets. But the larger model was too large to run on those weak devices itself, and it still relied on a separate server. This means the team did not show an AI worm capable of spreading and running itself on such devices. Anthropic argues that as small models become more capable, one could eventually use both methods.
The research also raises the prospect of adaptation and improvement by suggesting that AI models could subsist on low-power devices and drift through the Internet, getting better at spreading as they go. Anthropic makes this clear in its blog post about the work, concluding that AI systems could soon be “passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves.”
Ladish believes the main lesson from the research is in how AI models could divvy up work across computers of all shapes and sizes. “Basically, compute is a resource that these models can use,” he says, pointing to everything from Apple MacBooks to data centers to everyday objects like smart TVs as possible sources of computing power if attackers can hack them.
Not everyone thinks that the experiments amount to a new kind of threat, however. “I think there’s some caution that’s needed here to make sure we talk about what capabilities are new and transformative,” says Michael Bailey, a professor studying computer systems security at the Georgia Institute of Technology. He emphasizes avoiding “fearmongering” with the lessons taken away from this kind of work. Researchers already know how insecure devices like TV boxes can be. “We already had self-replicating malware,” says Bailey. “We had botnets.”
“All of these are classical computer security threats,” adds Vyas Sekar, a professor of computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University. According to Sekar, the bigger problem is that more people might be able to launch such attacks—a “democratization of being evil,” as he calls it. Sekar thinks this makes monitoring and restricting data flow between smart devices even more important.
Even the risk of hijacking raw computing power on chips is not new. Hackers have long taken over other people’s computers to mine cryptocurrency. So while smart devices could face new attacks of the kind Anthropic describes, the underlying weakness is an old one: plenty of our gadgets are already easy to commandeer.

indian-startups-f7e2a939ff.headline: Inside SEBI’s 10 Key Proposed Changes To SME IPO Rules
indian-startups-f7e2a939ff.fulltext: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has proposed sweeping changes to the rules governing initial public offerings (IPOs) of small and medium enterprises (SMEs). In a consultation paper floated on October 14, the markets regulator has proposed changes to SME IPO norms, including regulations pertaining to valuation thresholds, profitability and shareholder exits. The regulator has invited public feedback on the paper till November 4. Citing its rationale, the regulator said that the paper has been formulated by its working group due to rapid increase in the funds raised through SME IPOs and the number of investors participating in such issues. Since launch in 2012, about 1,500 companies have opted to list on the SME platform and have raised ₹40,222 Cr. Startups like Zappfresh, DroneAcharya, TAC Infosec, Yudiz, are a few startups that have also taken this route to go public. In view of this, the regulator has proposed multiple changes, including lowering the minimum application threshold and removing mandatory underwriting and market-making requirements. Here’s a look at some of the key changes that have been proposed: The Market Cap-Based Listing Criteria Under the proposed framework, companies with a post-issue market capitalisation of ₹1,000 Cr or less can now list on the SME platform. Those valued in the range of ₹1,000 Cr to ₹4,000 Cr can also choose to list either on the SME platform or the main board. Companies valued over ₹4,000 Cr will have to list on the main board. SEBI has also proposed replacing the existing paid-up share capital criterion with post-issue market capitalisation to determine whether a company can list on the SME platform or the main board. Currently, companies with post-issue paid-up share capital of up to ₹25 Cr can opt for the SME platform, subject to other eligibility conditions. In addition, companies in the ₹1,000 Cr to ₹4,000 Cr band choosing the SME platform would also have to submit restated consolidated financial statements under Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) for the preceding three financial years, if they have not already adopted Ind AS. If an IPO applicant’s estimated market capitalisation crosses the applicable threshold during the IPO process, it would have to refile under the relevant listing framework. Minimum Profitability Requirements Raised SEBI has proposed mandating SME IPO applicants to report an average operating profit of at least ₹3 Cr annually over the preceding three financial years, based on restated consolidated financial statements. In contrast, the existing framework requires operating profit of at least ₹1 Cr in at least two of the preceding three fiscal years. However, the consultation paper refers to EBIT in its narrative, while existing provision mentioned EBITDA. This requires clarification. Companies that fail the proposed profitability test could still list on the SME platform through an alternative route. They would have to use the book-building process and allocate at least 75% of the net offer to qualified institutional buyers (QIBs). If the required allocation is not achieved, the entire subscription amount would have to be refunded. New Rules For Converted And Reorganised Businesses SEBI has proposed changing the eligibility rules for SMEs seeking an IPO after converting from a proprietorship, partnership or limited liability partnership (LLP). These draft rules also cover companies undergoing qualifying business reorganisations. Currently, such companies generally need to complete at least one full financial year before filing their draft IPO papers. Under the new proposal, they would need to complete four consecutive financial quarters from the date of conversion or qualifying reorganisation and submit at least one annual audited financial statement prepared after the change. The proposal also covers acquisitions, succession and schemes of arrangement, where more than 50% of the revenue comes from businesses that previously operated as proprietorships, partnerships or LLPs. In such cases, the earlier business' operating track record could be considered when assessing IPO eligibility. The ₹10 Cr Cap On GCP Allocation May Go SEBI has proposed removing the ₹10 Cr cap on the amount that the companies can allocate, from their IPO proceeds, towards general corporate purposes (GCP). Currently, GCP allocation cannot exceed 15% of the amount raised or ₹10 Cr, whichever is lower. Under the proposal, the 15% limit would remain, but the fixed ₹10 Cr ceiling would be removed, allowing companies raising larger amounts to allocate more funds to general business needs. SEBI Looks To Reshuffle OFS Rules SEBI has also proposed a dedicated offer-for-sale (OFS) framework with a one-year holding requirement, subject to specified exemptions. The draft framework also seeks to remove the existing 20% ceiling on the OFS component for qualified institutional buyers (QIBs). The Primary Market Advisory Committee (PMAC) went a step further and suggested removing the 50% cap on a QIB’s pre-issue holding as well. These exemptions, however, would not apply to companies using the alternative listing route after failing the proposed profitability test. Lock-In Periods To Be Revised SEBI has proposed revising the lock-in periods for promoters and other shareholders after an SME IPO. The draft changes include: Minimum promoters' contribution: The three-year lock-in on minimum promoter contribution would begin from the IPO allotment date. In contrast, the lock-in date is currently linked to the commencement of commercial production. Promoter holdings above the minimum contribution: The existing staggered lock-in would be replaced with a uniform one-year lock-in. Non-promoter pre-issue capital: The lock-in will reduce from the current one year to six months. Promoter group holdings: A separate one-year lock-in would apply from the IPO allotment date. Depositories could also mark shares that cannot be locked in electronically as non-transferable for the applicable period. SEBI to Further Trim Minimum IPO Application Threshold The markets regulator has proposed lowering the minimum application amount for SME IPOs to ₹1 Lakh from the existing requirement of more than ₹2 Lakh. Investors would have to apply for at least four lots worth a minimum of ₹25,000 each. The ₹2 Lakh minimum was introduced in March 2025 to limit participation by smaller retail investors. The consultation paper also proposes aligning investor categories and allocation rules more closely with the mainboard framework, including the introduction of the ‘Retail Individual Investor’ category. Under the regime, Issuers can also allocate up to 60% of the QIB portion to anchor investors in book-built issues. SEBI has also proposed increasing the minimum number of allottees from 200 to 500. Under the alternative route for companies failing the profitability test, up to 10% of the net offer would go to retail investors, up to 15% to NIIs and at least 75% to QIBs. SME Shares Could Be Traded In Lots Of One SEBI has proposed allowing investors to trade SME-listed shares in lots of one share, replacing the existing price-linked lot sizes. The consultation paper notes that around 5% of unique PAN-based shareholders held odd-lot shares, on average. The proposed change could make it easier for investors to sell their entire holdings, but it will not change the minimum IPO application amount. End For Mandatory Underwriting And Market-Making? SEBI has proposed removing mandatory underwriting and market-making requirements for SME IPOs to reduce listing costs. Currently, SME IPOs must be fully underwritten, with lead managers required to underwrite at least 15% of the issue themselves. Under the proposal, these requirements would be removed. The 75% QIB portion under the alternative listing route would not need to be underwritten. Underwriting fees accounted for 49.52% and 38.41% of total SME IPO issue expenses on the NSE in FY25 and FY26, respectively. The corresponding figures for the BSE were 32.20% and 33.99%, according to SEBI. The minimum subscription requirement would remain at 90% of the offer, excluding OFS. If the threshold is not met, application money would have to be refunded within four days of the issue closing. SEBI has also proposed removing the requirement to maintain market-makers for three years after listing. Market-making fees accounted for 1.25%-4.20% of total issue expenses across the NSE and BSE in FY25 and FY26. The change could reduce costs but may affect liquidity in SME stocks with limited trading activity. Changes To Mainboard Migration Rules SEBI has proposed revising the rules that govern SME-listed companies, when they move to the mainboard. Under the proposed framework, companies with a market capitalisation of ₹1,000 Cr or less would not have to migrate solely because of their valuation. Those valued above ₹1,000 Cr but below ₹4,000 Cr could voluntarily migrate, subject to the main board's eligibility criteria. Companies valued at ₹4,000 Cr or more would have to mandatorily migrate. Board approval would be sufficient for migration, without a shareholder vote. SEBI has also proposed removing the requirement to migrate when paid-up capital is likely to exceed ₹25 Cr and scrapping migration from the main board to the SME platform. Companies already listed on the SME platform, when the new rules are notified, would continue to follow the existing migration framework.

climate-energy-876da088f4.headline: India Curtails 1.46 Billion Units Of Solar Power In 2 Months
climate-energy-876da088f4.fulltext:
Markets
India Curtails 1.46 Billion Units Of Solar Power In 2 Months
Solar generation grew 39% YoY in Q2 FY2026–27, but limited operational battery storage and grid constraints contributed to renewable energy curtailment, says CREA 
Key Takeaways
- CREA says solar accounted for 58% of the increase in renewable electricity generation during Q2 FY 2026-27
- It reached a daily record of 705 million units on September 30, 2026, yet India curtailed 1,462 million units of solar electricity in July and August, despite high power demand
- Insufficient battery storage capacity is also a challenge, with 9.1 GWh operational against 151 GWh of tendered battery storage projects as of August 2026
India’s solar power generation grew 39% year-on-year (YoY) in Q2 FY2026–27. However, grid and operational constraints, along with limited energy storage capacity, led to the curtailment of 1.46 billion units of solar electricity in July and August, despite high electricity demand, according to a report by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
India’s peak electricity demand reached 270 GW on July 16, 2026, up 18% from 230 GW in the same quarter a year earlier. Daily peak demand occurred during solar-generation hours on 62 of the quarter’s 92 days.
Despite record peak demand, India’s coal power plants operated at a 68% utilization rate in Q2 FY2026–27, according to CREA.
However, although solar was the fastest-growing major source of electricity generation during the quarter, with output reaching a record 705 million units (MU) on September 30, 2026, it was curtailed. This renewable energy source accounted for 58% of the increase in renewable electricity generation during the quarter.
Nevertheless, India’s solar capacity reached 168 GW as of August 2026, accounting for around 30% of the country’s total installed power capacity of 555 GW, next only to coal and lignite’s 231 GW. The latter accounted for 66% of the national generation mix even as plant-level stocks declined.
During the reporting quarter, in the months of July and August, India curtailed 1,462 MU of solar and 373 MU of wind capacity, out of 1,835 MU of renewable energy capacity curtailed.
In light of these findings, Manoj Kumar, India Analyst at CREA, argues that India must assess new thermal capacity against expected demand, renewable generation, and storage availability, as solar increasingly meets daytime electricity demand while storage helps meet evening and nighttime peaks.
“This will help avoid building capacity that could remain underutilised as India’s power system evolves,” added Kumar.
According to CREA’s report, titled Quarterly Energy Snapshot for India: Q2 2026–27, India had approximately 9.1 GWh of operational battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity as of the time of the report’s publication. Another 3 GWh is expected to be commissioned by December 2026. As of August 2026, storage projects totaling approximately 290 GWh had been tendered. This included 151 GWh of battery storage and 142 GWh of pumped hydro storage.
Storage contributed up to 5.5 GW during nighttime peak demand, up from 4.1 GW in the first quarter of fiscal 2026-27. The gap between the storage project pipeline and operational capacity is quite visible, since storage met only about 1% to 2% of national electricity demand during these periods.
In a recent report, Rubix Data Sciences said India will need up to INR 4.79 trillion in investment to meet its projected BESS requirement – 236.22 GWh by FY 2031-32 – as renewable capacity and peak power demand rise (see India BESS Demand Estimated To Reach 236 GWh By FY 2032).

climate-energy-6e22e45be1.headline: Green hydrogen, data centres to drive ninefold rise in combined power consumption in India by 2035: S&P Global
climate-energy-6e22e45be1.fulltext:
India’s electricity demand is expected to grow significantly by 2035, with consumption by data centres and green hydrogen production alone projected to rise nearly ninefold to around 240 terawatt-hours (TWh), reported The Economic Times, citing S&P Global.
Electricity demand is projected to grow at an annual rate of 5.56% between 2025 and 2035, compared with 2.47% for overall energy demand. Consequently, electricity’s share in India’s total energy consumption is expected to increase to nearly 25% by 2035 from around 19% in 2025, the ratings agency said.
The combined electricity consumption of data centres and green hydrogen production is projected to increase nearly ninefold to around 240 terawatt-hours (TWh) by 2035, making them significant sources of additional demand.
The shift towards electricity is already visible, with electric vehicles reducing dependence on fossil fuels. The trend is expected to gather pace as industries increasingly adopt electricity and green hydrogen in their production processes.
Industrial expansion, higher household incomes, greater ownership of electrical appliances and rising cooling requirements are also expected to support growth in power consumption.
While the electricity grid will remain the main source of supply, distributed generation is expected to account for a larger share of electricity consumption. Its contribution could rise to around 16% by 2035 from approximately 13% in 2025, S&P Global said.
The agency warned that rising consumption and less predictable demand patterns would place additional pressure on India’s power infrastructure. Meeting future requirements would call for a diversified energy mix, stronger transmission and distribution networks, greater storage capacity and more flexible generation and electricity market arrangements.
S&P Global also noted that India had achieved its 2030 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) target of 50% cumulative installed power capacity from non-fossil fuel sources ahead of schedule. The country has set a higher target of 60% for 2035.
However, the agency cautioned that achieving capacity targets ahead of schedule would shift the focus towards ensuring that the power system can reliably integrate and deliver electricity from these sources.

global-economics-38e280ffd4.headline: CoreWeaves slump spotlights growing burden of debt behind AI boom
global-economics-38e280ffd4.fulltext:
ReutersPublished16 Oct 2026, 01:28 AM IST
By Aditya Soni, Anhata Rooprai and Laura Matthews
Oct 15 (Reuters) - Shares of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave steadied on Thursday after a sharp slump, as investors worried about the debt financing behind the artificial intelligence build-out.
The loss-making cloud company has about $50 billion in debt and has become a focus of concerns that the data-center boom is being fueled by credit, straining newer players and pressuring cash flows even at giants such as Alphabet and Meta Platforms.
CoreWeave's slump fueled a global rout in AI stocks, underscoring investor doubts about whether future revenue from the technology can keep pace with the spending.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company is CoreWeave's second-largest investor with about a 10% stake, played down the fears. "CoreWeave’s financial strength is improving every day," Huang told reporters at a Stockholm event, adding that he does not see a need for Nvidia to backstop the company. "I'm optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing."
CoreWeave stock was last up 5% after slipping as much as 8.3% to its lowest level since May 2025.
"The market is waking up to the fact that AI demand and a profitable business model are two very different things," said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group.
"It looks more like investors questioning how the build-out is being funded than a sudden collapse in appetite for AI computing. But if the cost of capital keeps rising, even strong demand may not be enough to protect the most heavily leveraged players."
The jitters come as investors await Anthropic's IPO, which would be a test of whether the Claude AI model maker's rapid revenue growth can ease worries about runaway AI spending.
The market selloff has already led some companies such as smart ring maker Oura to push back their listings.
The yield on CoreWeave's April-issued bonds was trading around 15% on Thursday, above the level that typically signals distress, drawing a "yikes" from Elon Musk on social media. The bond was last down 0.3 cents on the dollar to 79.15 cents, according to Tradeweb data.
The cost of insuring its debt against default has climbed to around 1,000 basis points, implying a nearly 63% chance of default in five years, up from about 30% a year ago. That is despite a deal under which Nvidia will buy any unsold CoreWeave capacity through April 13, 2032.
Options traders also ramped up bearish bets. Volume in put options, which give investors the right to sell shares at a certain price, hit a record high on Wednesday, according to Chris Murphy, co-head of derivatives strategy at Susquehanna.
“People are using put options to hedge negative credit sentiment, and we've seen consistent and aggressive put buying all week,” Murphy said.
Investors bought contracts that would profit if CoreWeave shares fell below $42.50, $50, and $60 in the coming weeks, while others used more complex trades to reduce the cost of some of those bearish wagers by taking on some risk tied to much lower share-price levels later in the year, according to Murphy and TradeAlert data.
CoreWeave, which went public in March 2025, leads newer cloud providers known as neoclouds that rent out computing power from scarce and costly Nvidia processors to meet soaring demand, often borrowing heavily to buy the chips. It counts Microsoft and OpenAI among its customers, according to media reports.
That leaves neoclouds exposed to any cooling in AI demand, critics have said, while the chips lose value as newer ones arrive, forcing another round of heavy spending to replace them.
CoreWeave raised its annual capital spending forecast by $4 billion to as much as $39 billion in August. It is expected to post revenue of nearly $13 billion this year and a loss of $2.13 billion, according to analysts' estimates.
Worries about the build-out, on which US tech giants are expected to spend more than $700 billion this year, have in recent days rippled through the stocks that have been the biggest winners since ChatGPT's November 2022 launch.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, a closely watched gauge of chip stocks, has erased over $1.6 trillion in market value in an 11.6% slide over the past six sessions. The Nasdaq has declined more than 3% in the period.
On Thursday, tech shares fell across Asia, Europe and the US, dragging broader markets lower on fears that rising interest rates could hurt the sector.
'UNLIMITED' POOLS OF CAPITAL
The CoreWeave selloff came as its co-founder Brannin McBee told the Financial Times that the company was seeking an investment-grade rating that would open the door to "unlimited" capital.
The same day research firm Gartner said about 80% of neoclouds could shut down by 2030 and that more than $3.5 trillion of AI spending could face impairment if AI providers keep up their current pace of investment.
"In 2026, AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on AI infrastructure, and are forecast to invest an additional $6 trillion between 2027 and 2030," said Will Sommer, analyst at Gartner.
"However, our research indicates enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures during this period."
CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator pushed back on the concerns in an internal memo on Wednesday seen by Reuters, telling employees the company's deal backlog more than covers its debt obligations and that markets can sometimes "misunderstand and act irrationally".
(Reporting by Aditya Soni, Anhata Rooprai and Shashwat Chauhan in Bengaluru; Editing by Sweta Singh, Saumyadeb Chakrabarty, Arun Koyyur, Megan Davies and Sanjeev Miglani)

global-economics-9d2e8a0b76.headline: Indian mutual funds stop bulk subscriptions to gold ETFs ahead of festive season
global-economics-9d2e8a0b76.fulltext:
ReutersPublished16 Oct 2026, 12:26 AM IST
By Ira Dugal and Rajendra Jadhav
MUMBAI, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Several large Indian mutual funds issued public notices late on Thursday suspending bulk subscriptions to gold exchange-traded funds, just ahead of the festive season when investor demand typically rises.
The notices from the fund houses, including Kotak Mahindra Mutual Fund, UTI Mutual Fund and HDFC Mutual Fund, did not cite a reason for the move. There is no restriction on redemptions from these funds.
The decision was taken following a nudge from the Securities and Exchange Board of India, according to a mutual fund executive familiar with the discussions. Two bullion industry officials confirmed the halt had followed discussions with the market regulator.
The sources declined to be identified as they are not permitted to comment on discussions with the regulator.
A spokesperson for SEBI did not respond to a Reuters request for comment outside business hours.
The Indian rupee has been under pressure this year due to a surge in global oil prices, which have inflated the country's import bill, and heavy selling by foreign investors in Indian equities. Strong demand for gold has further weighed on the currency, prompting the government to raise import duties on gold and silver earlier this year.
India, the world's largest consumer of silver and second-largest consumer of gold, relies on imports to meet most of its demand, a dependence that can sometimes widen its trade deficit.
Gold imports fell to $1.8 billion in September, from $2.3 billion in August. However, Indians will celebrate Dussehra in October and Diwali in early November, when buying gold is considered auspicious.
Inflows into gold and silver ETFs surged during last year's festive season as investors turned to precious metals amid lackluster stock market returns.
The move is surprising, as gold and silver imports have fallen sharply over the past two months from a year earlier and have not contributed to the trade deficit, said a dealer at a private bank that supplies bullion to ETFs.
"It looks more like a precautionary measure to avoid a surge in imports in October," the dealer said.
(Reporting by Ira Dugal and Rajendra Jadhav in Mumbai; Editing by Shilpi Majumdar)

health-tech-505cc42c54.headline: ‘AI lowers the capital needed’: India’s drug discovery push faces test of human trials
health-tech-505cc42c54.fulltext:
‘AI lowers the capital needed’: India’s drug discovery push faces test of human trials
Indian scientists and biopharmaceutical firms are using artificial intelligence to identify promising drug candidates faster and at lower cost. But industry experts tell CNA the technology can address only part of a lengthy and risky development process.
NEW DELHI: A team of about a dozen people at Indian drug-discovery startup Peptris is using artificial intelligence to work on more than a dozen potential drug programmes simultaneously.
Peptris co-founder Venkatasubramanian Narayanan said the company advanced one of its drug development programmes to a late preclinical stage in about 18 months, compared with more than four years using conventional methods.
Such fast development could signal a fundamental shift in India’s pharmaceutical sector, helping it to expand beyond its traditional focus and areas of success.
Industry scientists told CNA that India has historically been strongest in generics, manufacturing and contract research for international firms, while original drug discovery remains less developed.
The scale of India’s pharmaceutical industry was highlighted at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi on Tuesday, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the country supplies one in every five generic medicines used globally.
The government is now investing in drug discovery efforts.
In September, India’s Department of Pharmaceuticals approved about 16 billion rupees (US$168 million) in funding for 41 pharmaceutical and medical technology research projects, including novel drug discovery and clinical development.
Drug developers and scientists say that AI could make it cheaper and faster for more Indian companies to develop their own medicines by identifying promising compounds earlier.
But that addresses only part of the challenge.
Noubar Afeyan, co-founder and chairman of US-based pharma giant Moderna, told CNA that India’s ability to turn promising science into medicines will depend on building much more of the infrastructure needed before and during human trials.
“It’s probably more important to get preclinical and clinical capabilities established at scale than just AI,” he said. “I don’t think AI will fix that.”
LOWERING THE BARRIERS TO DRUG DISCOVERY
The potential significance goes beyond India’s pharmaceutical exports - which rose by 2.1 per cent to about US$31 billion in the financial year ended March 2026, according to government data.
Non-communicable diseases accounted for 49 per cent of deaths in India in 2021, or about 6.4 million, according to the World Health Organization. The financial burden is also significant, with households paying 43.4 per cent of the country’s total health expenditure out of pocket in financial year 2022-23, according to India’s National Health Accounts.
Scientists said that lower research costs could help more Indian companies develop new treatments without the resources of a large pharmaceutical firm.
Megha Goyal, a drug-discovery scientist and co-founder of Abhinavayan Biotech, said AI is already helping smaller Indian biotechnology companies identify promising drug targets, screen potential compounds and design molecules before committing to laboratory experiments.
“AI has not made drug discovery easy; it has made it more accessible and more efficient,” she said.
Peptris’ Narayanan said Indian scientists and contract research organisations already perform sophisticated drug-discovery work, even if Indian companies have historically taken on less of the financial risk involved in owning the medicines being developed.
Goyal said the bigger challenge for Indian drug developers comes after the initial discovery stage.
“Drug discovery is inherently a long-term and high-risk endeavour that requires patient capital, sustained commitment [and] long-term vision,” she said.
Vishesh Rajaram, founding partner at venture capital firm Speciale Invest, said he is now seeing more scientists build companies around drugs of their own rather than provide research services or manufacture existing medicines.
“Today we see (Indian) scientist-founders building novel-chemistry, biologics and AI-first discovery companies with global ambitions from day one,” said Rajaram, whose firm has invested in Peptris.
He said cheaper computing and AI tools can reduce the number of compounds researchers need to make and physically test, allowing smaller teams to identify promising drug candidates with less money.
But Rajaram said those savings are concentrated largely at the beginning of drug development.
“AI lowers the capital needed to create an asset,” he said. “It doesn’t yet lower the capital needed to prove that the asset works in patients.”
THE HARD PART
Santanu Datta, co-founder and chief scientific officer at Bengaluru-based biopharma firm Bugworks, said AI works best with large amounts of reliable data. This includes the shape of a molecule, its intended target and how similar compounds have behaved.
A drug may appear to interact with its intended target as hoped, but behave differently in patients, affect other proteins or cause unforeseen effects, said Dutta.
He compared it to predicting how a person behaves alone versus trying to predict what happens when that person is placed in a crowded city.
“Once you put the person in a city with a million people, things change,” he said.
Datta has spent more than three decades in drug discovery, including more than 20 years working on infectious diseases at AstraZeneca India.
Bugworks, which he later co-founded, is developing treatments for drug-resistant infections and cancer, and its lead antibiotic has progressed to Phase 1 human trials - the first stage of testing an experimental drug in people, primarily to assess its safety.
But there is still a long road to an approved drug. Only 7.9 per cent of drug programmes that entered Phase 1 trials between 2011 and 2020 ultimately received approval, according to an analysis by the Biotechnology Innovation Organization, Informa Pharma Intelligence and QLS Advisors.
According to the United States Food and Drug Administration, a medicine typically passes through three phases of clinical human trials before regulators decide whether to approve it.
“From idea to drug candidate, there are massive improvements (using AI),” Afeyan of Moderna said. “From drug candidate to human proof of concept, there are smaller improvements.”
Another challenge is that large pharmaceutical companies have years of data from failed drug programmes that could help AI identify what is unlikely to work, but much of it remains private, Datta said.
‘VERY NASCENT STAGE’
There are early signs that Indian companies are beginning to create novel drug candidates that attract interest beyond the country.
Peptris, for example, has licensed one of its drug candidates to US-based pharma firm Revio Therapeutics for further development, giving it an overseas partner to take the programme forward.
Industry executives said how far Indian companies can develop their own drugs before seeking partners will determine how much value India retains.
Speciale Invest’s Rajaram said licensing Indian-developed drugs overseas was “a genuine step up, but not yet the destination”. A bigger shift, he said, would come when more Indian companies take their own treatments into early human trials before seeking larger partners.
Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, founder of Indian biopharmaceutical major Biocon, said it was still too early to conclude that AI was transforming drug development in the country.
“We are still at a very nascent stage, and nothing of this is proven,” she said. “Proof of concept at pilot scale is no reflection on what is really the true opportunity at scale.”

global-economics-9ea972ef1e.headline: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt
global-economics-9ea972ef1e.fulltext:
An accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, as fears over rising inflation and future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.
Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5% respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.
Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in the memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI.
The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where the Nasdaq Composite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, its worst performance since July.
US stocks fell further when trading resumed on Thursday. The Nasdaq dropped another 1.4% at the start of trading, with Dell, which makes datacentre servers, and Coherent, which manufactures components for AI datacentres, leading the early fallers.
The sell-off came after US data on Wednesday showed stateside inflation jumped to a higher-than-expected 3.7% in September, marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May.
Fresh data on Thursday showing US producers increased their prices by 6.3% year on year in September – the sharpest rise since December 2022 – added to inflationary jitters.
The figures have rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month.
“Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid said.
Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.”
The sell-off follows warnings from the International Monetary Fund, which said this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets was putting world financial stability at risk.
“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” the IMF said. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit.
The latest jitters hit China, where the Shanghai Shenzhen CSI 300 slipped by as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits.
European stocks also came under pressure, with Germany’s DAX down 0.36% in afternoon trading and the Italian FTSE MIB dropping by 1.3%.

DRDO successfully tests quantum-secured communication to shield sensitive military data
NEW DELHI: Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) on Wednesday said it has successfully configured and tested a Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) platform in the live network of the dynamic test ranges at Proof and Experimental Establishment (PXE), Chandipur, thereby advancing India’s capabilities in quantum-secured communications.QKD is a secure communication method that uses the laws of quantum mechanics to let two parties generate a shared and secret random key known only to them, which then can be used to encrypt and decrypt messages.According to DRDO, this demonstrates the adept use case of QKD to fortify the real-time critical observations and telemetry associated with artillery and armoured weapon tests and evaluation. QKD has been designed and developed under microelectronic devices, computational systems and cyber security (MCC) cluster of DRDO with production partner Taqbit labs and will aptly provide unconditional security, along with eavesdropping detection. QKD uses unique properties of quantum mechanical systems to generate and distribute cryptographic keying material using special-purpose technology.Quantum communication provides fundamentally unbreakable encryption, making it a dual-use technology with applications in securing data in strategic sectors such as defence, finance, and telecommunications, as well as in protecting national security-related communications.

October 15, 2026

The United States International Trade Commission (USITC) has ruled that imports of crystalline silicon photovoltaic (PV) cells, whether assembled into modules or not, from India, Indonesia, and Laos materially injured the domestic solar manufacturing industry.
Following the USITC’s affirmative determination, the Department of Commerce will issue antidumping and countervailing duty orders on November 2, 2026, on the covered solar products imported from India, Indonesia, and Laos.
The determination follows the US Department of Commerce’s September findings that solar products imported from the three countries were sold in the U.S. at less than fair value and benefited from government subsidies.
In its final affirmative determinations, Commerce finalized a dumping margin of 123.04% on Indian solar cell exporters. The companies include Mundra Solar PV, Mundra Solar Energy, Kowa Company, Premier Energies Photovoltaic, and all other unnamed exporters.
In the countervailing duty investigation, Commerce determined a subsidy rate of 126.09% for Mundra Solar Energy and Mundra Solar PV. It applied the same rate to all other Indian exporters and producers.
The USITC’s October 14 determination completes the injury assessment required for the imposition of the trade remedies.
The investigations followed petitions filed on July 17, 2025, by the Alliance for American Solar Manufacturing and Trade, comprising First Solar, Hanwha Q CELLS USA, and Mission Solar Energy.
The Department of Commerce initiated antidumping and countervailing duty investigations in August 2025 to examine the allegations.
In February 2026, Commerce announced preliminary affirmative countervailing duty determinations for solar imports from the three countries. For India, it assigned a preliminary subsidy rate of 125.87% to Mundra Solar Energy and Mundra Solar PV and applied the same rate to other exporters.
In April 2026, Commerce announced preliminary affirmative antidumping determinations. It assigned a dumping margin of 123.04% to Mundra Solar Energy and Mundra Solar PV.
